19.0.0.en: Pilate wavered between the voice of truth (conscience) and the weakness of the Jews and the ferocity of their cry for Christ's crucifixion, so he first handed Him over to scourging, hoping to calm the Jews' uproar; and St. Luke affirms this in (Lk 23:16): "I will therefore chastise him, and release him." Matthew and Mark both mention the scourging and crucifixion together (Mt 27:26; Mk 15:15), but St. John separated them, as well as Pilate's feeble attempts to acquit Christ. And St. John moves to the scene of the Roman soldiers' mockery of Christ during the scourging: they ridiculed Him and put on Him a robe whose color represented the garments of kings, and they also plaited a crown of thorns and crowned Him with it (see Isa 53:5).

19.0.1.en: "And they smote him with their hands": and Matthew adds (Mt 27:30) that they struck Him on the head, and we do not think there is a tongue or a writer who can describe or express this wicked scene...

19.0.2.en: But we are content to ask the Lord of glory: Why, my God, did You endure the hands of wicked sinners being stretched out against Your righteous, holy face, and how can this happen?!

19.0.3.en: And His answer comes: For your salvation, my child!!!

19.0.4.en: In an attempt to clear his conscience, Pilate goes out and declares a second time the innocence of Christ, but it is a declaration without a verdict to that effect.

19.1.0.en: Pilate brought Jesus out after the scourging, wearing the purple and with the thorns on His head, in a last attempt to win the sympathy of the Jews so that he might release Christ. But they grew more hardened and demanded His crucifixion, so Pilate gave his third testimony to the innocence of Jesus (see ch. 18:38; 19:4-6). And in an attempt to warn the Jews, Pilate wanted to rid his hands of responsibility, so he said to them: "Take ye him, and crucify him," without involving me in your crime.

19.2.0.en: The Jews presented their first accusation, that Christ was an evildoer (ch. 18:30), and when they failed, they presented the second accusation, that He was a traitor to Caesar, and Christ repelled this accusation from Himself when He answered that His kingdom is not of this world (ch. 8:36). And here the Jews came with a third accusation, that He was a blasphemer of the Law, that is, their religion, and according to it He must die, and by this they nullify Pilate's defense of Christ, that he finds no fault in Him.

19.3.0.en: Pilate was frightened when the Jews mentioned that Christ is "the Son of God," and we may understand why: he was afraid of passing sentence on an innocent man whom he did not condemn in anything, but he sensed the Jews' plot and cruelty that were leading him in the current toward sentencing Him, and he was also afraid of the words "Son of God," since the Romans and Greeks believed in the possibility of the gods appearing and becoming incarnate or begetting offspring ... Perhaps Christ was one of the sons of the gods, so would Pilate bring himself into enmity with the gods? We add to that another reason for his fright, which was the dream his wife dreamed and told him of, saying to him: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man" (Mt 27:19).

19.4.0.en: In an attempt to overcome his fright and fear, Pilate took Jesus inside to inquire of Him: "Whence art thou?" Is it from heaven?! Are you a son of the gods as I have heard? And Christ's not answering is the conviction of His blessed person that what He says would not change the situation at all, and what Pilate had heard from Him was enough for him to acquit Him. And to push Christ to speak, Pilate threatened Him with his authority to kill Him or release Him.

19.4.1.en: So there came Christ's strong answer, which frightened Pilate: "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above." The crucifixion, then, is the will of the Father and the consent and submission of the Son, and no earthly or temporal authority has power to control it, and at the same time, Pilate was not relieved of responsibility because he was hesitant and passive, and did not declare His innocence. "But he that delivered me unto thee," that is, Judas and the Jews, out of envy, "hath the greater sin" than yours; and perhaps the reason for the lessening of Pilate's sin is that he was a Gentile who did not know the Scriptures and the promises as these men knew them.

19.5.0.en: We do not know how Pilate sought to release Christ, whether by talks with the crowd or some of the chief priests. But it is certain that his fright and perplexity increased before his conscience and his examination of Jesus on the one hand, and before the shouting of the Jews and their threatening on the other, so they threatened him with what he had not counted on, which is that if he released one who claims to be a king of the Jews, he would implicitly agree to the existence of a king other than Caesar, and this we do not accept, and it would also make you a traitor to Caesar. The Jews thereby succeeded in bringing a new kind of fear into his heart, which was the fear for his political position and being an enemy of Caesar himself.

19.6.0.en: Pilate brought the Lord Jesus out of the judgment hall to the courtyard where the Jews were waiting, and sat on his seat that the Roman governors used when issuing their judgments. And St. John adds, to involve us in the scene, the place and position of the seat, for it was on a raised hill (Gabbatha) relative to the courtyard where the Jews had gathered, and it is also called (the Pavement) because it was paved with marble and alabaster.

19.7.0.en: And as it approached the sixth hour, and only three hours remained until the offering of the Passover (at the ninth), Pilate had to take a decision about Christ, so he tried for the last time to rid himself of the decision and leave the Jews to judge Him, saying: "Behold your King!"

19.8.0.en: Pilate's saying "Behold your King!" provoked the Jews and their agitation increased, and they answered him: "Take him, why do you give him to us? Take him and crucify him." And when he asked them: "Shall I crucify your King?" they cried out: "We have no king but Caesar." This is a denial and a renunciation ... for the Jews know that they have no king but God, and that the Romans occupy them, and they were waiting for deliverance from them.

19.8.1.en: But now to declare that their king is Caesar, they are thereby an example of the person who changes all his principles in a moment because of malice in his heart, and thereby they applied the principle "the end justifies the means." And the end of the feeble trial scene came with the submission of one who feared for his position because of the riot: let one die even if innocent so that I may save myself; and what a principle!!!

19.8.2.en: Beloved reader, it is easy for us here to criticize Pilate for misusing his authority, and for his fear and cowardice. But in other situations in our daily life, may we not lie to escape from an act for which we deserve rebuke, or evade the responsibility of declaring the truth, trying to wash our hands and throw the responsibility on others as Pilate did, or do like the Jews: find a justification for our evils with which we numb our consciences?! Have mercy on us, O Lord.

19.9.0.en: That is, from the judgment hall first, then from Jerusalem second, to be crucified outside the camp (Golgotha). And St. Paul speaks of this: "Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate. Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach" (Heb 13:12-13).

19.9.1.en: And note, dear reader, that our Church, in bringing out this spiritual meaning, took care in the rite of Holy Week to leave the sanctuary and the choir of the deacons and pray in the nave of the church, to go out with Christ outside Jerusalem.

19.9.2.en: "Skull, Golgotha": the tradition inherited among the Jews said that it was the place where the skull of Adam was buried. But scholars describe it as a hill of moderate height, whose rocky form resembles a skull in its structure, and this place was used for stoning and was near the city.

19.10.0.en: St. John referred to the crucifixion briefly, and mentioned the two robbers without mentioning the dialogue with Christ. Therefore, to review the events of the crucifixion, see the texts (Mt 27; Mk 15; Lk 23) in the parts concerning the events of the crucifixion to complete the whole picture.

19.11.0.en: There used to be written on the cross the name of the crucified and the reason for his crucifixion. St. John mentions here that what was written was first by the order of Pilate personally, and second in the Hebrew language of the Jews, the Greek language of thought and learning, and the Latin language of the official state. Because the place was elevated, and many of the people read it, the chief priests objected to the declaration that Christ was their king, because in this was a condemnation of them for killing their king. But this objection was met coldly by Pilate, and he insisted on his word that Christ is the King of the Jews. We do not know whether this was out of spite toward the chief priests, or out of reverence for a person in whom he saw no evil.

19.12.0.en: St. John was the one who made the story of the dividing of the garments clearest to us, so we understand that they were four soldiers, each of whom took a part. But the coat was woven and could not be divided, so they cast lots among themselves for whose it should be. And St. John reminds us, as Matthew also did (Mt 27:35), of what David said in his prophecies about the sufferings of the Cross: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture" (Ps 22:18).

19.13.s.en: (3) The words of the crucifixion and death

19.13.0.en: Who were the women whom the Holy Bible mentions at the Cross?! By reviewing the texts of all the Gospels we conclude that they were the Virgin Mary first, and "Salome," her cousin, second, as Mark mentioned her in his Gospel (Mk 15:40; 16:1), and as Matthew referred to her (Mt 20:20) as the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who is the mother of St. John; and the third of the women is Mary the wife of Clopas, the mother of James the Less and Joses; and the last of them is Mary Magdalene, whom Matthew mentioned in his Gospel first because of her piety after her repentance (Mt 27:56). And note that St. John did not mention the name of his mother, so as not to depart from his habitual practice of not mentioning his own name.

19.14.0.en: In the midst of His sufferings and crucifixion, and at His hardest moments, He did not forget His mother according to the flesh, the holy Virgin Mary. Since she had no sons according to the flesh but Him, Christ gave John to her as a son, and Christ charged John with the responsibility of caring for His mother; and the evangelist makes clear the response of both parties to Christ's commandment, since the beloved disciple took her to his own home.

19.14.1.en: But why was John the one who received this honor? Was he not, dear friend, the only one remaining in the midst of all the sufferings while others fled?!

19.14.2.en: My friend, St. John received the honor of hosting the Mother of God in his house because he did not leave the cross of the Lord of glory, for there is a special gift for everyone who does not flee from his cross, but receives it from God with joy.

19.15.0.en: "After this": it carries more than one meaning:

19.15.1.en: The first: that is, after the three hours of darkness.

19.15.2.en: The second: that is, after all the dialogues or words that took place on the Cross, whether John mentioned them or did not.

19.15.3.en: The third: that is, after He was assured of the handing over of St. Mary to John.

19.15.4.en: St. John pointed out that there were two final prophecies about the sufferings of Christ: "My tongue cleaveth to my jaws" (Ps 22:15), "and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" (Ps 69:21).

19.15.5.en: These two prophecies had to be fulfilled, so the Quencher of all humanity's thirst, in the blood of His love, cried out: "I thirst." Only John mentioned this vessel of vinegar, and this vinegar is wine that has begun to spoil, which is why it is called vinegar. The guards used to drink it because of its low price, or instead of throwing it away, so that it counted as free wine, and the guards took a stalk of the hyssop plant (its branches were used for sprinkling holy water according to Jewish rites) to bring the sponge soaked with vinegar to the mouth of Christ. This vinegar was different from the first vinegar, mixed with myrrh, which was used to dull the senses of those about to undergo the sufferings of crucifixion; and this first one Christ refused to drink, that He might pass through the sufferings in full without alleviation.

19.15.6.en: "It is finished": that is, He accomplished what He came for, offering Himself as a sacrifice for sin and an atonement for our sins, and the word "It is finished" is the sixth word in the order of the words that Christ said on the Cross, which are in the following order:

19.15.7.en: 1) "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:24).

19.15.8.en: 2) "Woman, behold thy son! ... Behold thy mother!" (vv. 26, 27).

19.15.10.en: 4) "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Lk 23:43).

19.15.13.en: 7) "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit" (Lk 23:46).

19.16.0.en: "Because it was the preparation": that is, the state of utmost concern for the Passover celebrations. And the first Sabbath of Passover week was the holiest Sabbath of the year among the Jews, and this did not suit the presence of bodies hanging on the crosses. So the Jews asked Pilate's permission to break the legs, a tradition known for quickly finishing off the crucified, by increasing the loss of blood after the shattering of the legs, so that the Sabbath would not be defiled by the crucified remaining on their ground. And the soldiers carried out the task on the first and the last, but as for Jesus, no one approached Him, and they marveled that He had given up the spirit so quickly (see Mk 15:44), and to be more certain, one of the soldiers pierced His side and there came out blood and water.

19.16.1.en: The coming out of the blood and water: all the ancient Fathers of the Church paused before the "phenomenon" of the blood and water coming out of the pierced side of the Savior, a pause containing many reflections, of which we cite the following few: Chrysostom sees: "We were born of the water and fed from the blood. Therefore, when we approach the cup of the Eucharist, we drink from the very pierced side."

19.16.2.en: And St. Tertullian comes close to Chrysostom in his reflection, saying: "We are baptized by water and glorified by blood; we are called by water and chosen by blood; this is why His side was wounded; for whoever is washed with water is prepared to drink the blood." As for St. Ambrose and the scholar Origen, they agreed almost on one meaning: "After death blood is glorified and no water comes out of a body, but this had to happen, so that we may know that from the dead body of Christ all life came forth."

19.17.0.en: St. John refers to himself, as usual, with a veiled reference, and makes clear the reason for the legs of the Lord Jesus not being broken, and His side being pierced with the spear and the blood and water coming out, that we may believe in Christ, in whom the following prophecies were fulfilled:

19.17.1.en: (1) A bone of Him shall not be broken: this commandment was concerning the Passover lamb, which directly symbolizes the person of Christ, and it came in (Ex 12:46), and St. Paul also referred to it in (1 Cor 5:7) when he said: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us," and also the prophecy that David mentioned in (Ps 34:20): "He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken."

19.17.2.en: (2) "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced" (Zech 12:10): "And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem ... and they shall look upon me (Christ) whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn." That is, as John said before, that death had taken place, but it was the hand of God that moved the hand of the soldier to pierce the side of Christ, so that what the Father had declared before by the Holy Spirit concerning His Christ might be fulfilled.

19.17.3.en: And here we pause, beloved, for the pierced side of Christ is not only a proof of prophecy, but a sign of love that Christ bears in His body, besides the nails, so the pierced side became a source of hope and protection within it from all the wars of the wicked adversary. So if you ever doubt that you have no place in the bosom of Christ, remember the water of Baptism with which you were washed, and the flowing blood that comes forth, awaiting you on the altar, and your hopes will be renewed, and your heart will be kindled with hope in the love of Him who loved you.

19.18.0.en: Why did Christ choose Joseph of Arimathea from among His followers (disciples) to bury His body?

19.18.1.en: (1) He was rich and owned a new tomb in the same place as the crucifixion, according to the prophecy: "And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death" (Isa 53:9; Mt 27:57-60).

19.18.2.en: (2) He was an honourable counsellor of high standing, so he was able to go in to Pilate (Mk 15:43).

19.19.0.en: "And there came also Nicodemus ... and took the body of Jesus": the events and their sequence indicate a distribution of tasks, then their meeting together for the shrouding. Joseph went to Pilate and Nicodemus brought the requirements for the shrouding, and the two took the body together. St. John refers to Nicodemus as the one who first came to Jesus (see ch. 3), and he is the same one who tried to defend Jesus before the council of the rulers of the Jews in (ch. 7:50). What Nicodemus carried was myrrh, which is the sap of one of the well-known trees, used for cleansing or lessening pain, and was one of the embalming materials the Pharaohs used and the Jews took from them. As for the aloes, it is a powder made from a fragrant tree and has a sweet smell ... and the amount Nicodemus brought was a hundred minas, and the mina is a Roman measure of volume and weight taken from the Greeks, amounting in volume to about half a liter, and in weight equal to 340 grams.

19.19.1.en: "Wound it in linen clothes": they mixed a blend of perfumes and fragrant oils and put it on the body, then wrapped it in linen.

19.19.2.en: "As the manner of the Jews is": this means what they took from the Egyptians of the customs of embalming.

19.20.0.en: The tomb in which Christ was buried was new and hewn in a rock inside a garden owned by Joseph of Arimathea near the place of the crucifixion, which helped to complete the procedures of shrouding and burial quickly before the twelfth hour, which is six in the evening by our reckoning, so that they would not enter the great Sabbath. Perhaps the surrender of the Savior's body into the hands of those who shrouded Him is the last of the scenes of the humility of God, whom we shall see afterward in the glories of His Resurrection.

19.20.1.en: The visit to the empty tomb; the appearances of Christ after His resurrection
